<div class="banner"><strong>What we measured.</strong> We tested ways to find facts in past chats. We did not ask an AI model to write answers. Each question appears in more than one test, so test counts do not count people. We label scores from other studies and cost examples as such.</div>

## The question we test

**Which way of choosing context finds the most useful facts?** We test three methods: BM25 keyword search, keeping the latest chats, and a random choice. We set four limits on how many chat sessions each method can keep. These simple methods give us a starting point for testing the tool.

## What we found

At a limit of five sessions, BM25 raises mean evidence recall by **`r round(100*effects$gain[effects$dataset=='LoCoMo'],1)` percentage points on LoCoMo** and **`r round(100*effects$gain[effects$dataset=='LongMemEval-S'],1)` points on LongMemEval-S**. Both gains use the latest-chat method as the base. Recall is the share of source sessions with key facts that a method finds. We score both methods on the same set of questions. These gains do not show how well an AI would answer or how much time a person would save.

## What this means for the platform

A memory tool should keep links to its source text. It should track which facts are current and keep projects apart. This test checks how we find text. We still need to test conflicting facts, moves between tools, ease of use, and the answers an AI gives.
